newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Brit Biotech sees drug launch in 1998.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brit Biotech sees drug launch in 1998.

text.p: British Biotech Plc moved closer to its first drug launch as the British flagship biotech firm said on Wednesday it had applied for approval to market its Zacutex treatment against acute pancreatis in Europe.
The company hopes the European Medicines Evaluation Agency will give the green light for the drug in early 1998.
"Submitting the European Marketing Authorisation Application on target marks a landmark in the history of the company," chief executive Keith McCullagh said.
Clinical trials showed Zacutex helps to fight liver and kidney failure induced by acute pancreatitis, which kills up to 10 percent of all sufferers.
Some 100,000 people in western Europe and 200,000 in the U.S. suffer from acute pancreatis each year with no approved medicine on the market to treat the condition.
"Acute pancreatis is a life threatening condition and there are currently no approved therapies for it," a spokeswoman said.
"Therefore we would hope that the application would proceed quite rapidly."
Analysts have forecast Zacutex could eventually reach annual sales between $200 and $300 million. Late trials aimed at registration in the United States are still under way.
The Zacutex announcement came as British Biotech posted third quarter results showing losses narrowing to 1.55 million pounds ($2.50 million) from 4.05 million.
The results improved thanks to drug development payments from partner pharmaceutical companies Tanabe Seiyaku Co Ltd and Glaxo Wellcome Plc.

Tanabe Seiyaku Co Ltd, which develops and markets British Biotech's cancer drug marimastat in Japan, paid 4.4 million pounds, while Britain's Glaxo paid four million as a potential anti-arthritic drug will start human trials.
Development of marimastat, British Biotech's best known drug, is on track with four late trials completed or still under way. Another 14 tests are scheduled.
Marimastat is a new generation oral cancer drug which blocks the growth of tumours rather than actually killing them.
Some industry analysts have forecast the treatment could have sales of $4 billion a year.
British Biotech said Tanabe has up to a further $67 million to pay if marimastat proves successful in Japan.

The company said human trials will start in mid-1997 with BB-3644 to treat multiple sclerosis. Similar tests will start later in the year with BB-10153, which is a genetically engineered product to fight thrombosis.
British Biotech shares stood at 251-1/2 pence at 1330 gmt, up 1/2p from Tuesday's close. ($1=.6202 Pound)
